blurb: How machines learn to see — from sliding pattern-detectors to models that read photos and words together.

cards.title: How a computer starts to see

steps.h: An image is a grid of numbers
steps.p: To a computer, a photo is just a grid of pixels, each a few numbers for its red, green and blue brightness. A phone photo has millions of them.

visual.caption: Tiny patch of pixel brightness values (0 = black, 255 = white).

steps.p: A CNN slides small filters — say 3×3 pixels — across the whole image. Each filter lights up where it finds its pattern, like a vertical edge.
steps.analogy: Running a small stencil over every part of a page, noting where the shape fits.

steps.p: Early layers find edges. Later layers combine edges into textures and shapes, then shapes into parts like eyes or wheels, then whole objects.
The same filter is used at every position, so a cat is recognised whether it's top-left or bottom-right — with far fewer parameters.
A CNN called AlexNet, trained on GPUs, crushed a famous image-recognition contest in 2012 and kicked off the modern deep-learning boom.

cards.q: Why reuse the same filter at every position in an image?
options: A pattern is spotted anywhere, with far fewer parameters
It's needed to save the photo
cards.hint: A cat in the corner is still a cat.
cards.why: Find it anywhere, cheaply. One edge-detector works across the whole picture, instead of learning a separate one for every location.

cards.statement: CNNs assume nearby pixels are more related than distant ones.
cards.why: True. Small filters only look at neighbouring pixels. That built-in assumption fits real images well and helps CNNs learn from less data.

cards.title: AlexNet won the 2012 ImageNet contest with a 15.3% error rate — the runner-up had 26.2%.
cards.detail: That huge gap stunned the field, which quickly abandoned hand-designed image features for deep networks.

cards.q: What let 2015's ResNet train networks 152 layers deep?
options: Shortcut connections that add each block's input to its output
cards.why: Shortcuts. They let signals and corrections flow straight through many layers, so very deep networks stopped getting stuck during training.

cards.statement: ImageNet contains over 14 million labelled images.
cards.why: True. Built by Fei-Fei Li's team with crowdworkers labelling photos, it gave deep learning the data it needed to prove itself.

cards.title: Reading an image like a sentence

steps.p: A vision transformer chops an image into small squares — say 16×16 pixels — and treats each square like a word token.

visual.caption: A 224×224 image becomes a 14×14 grid = 196 patch tokens.

steps.p: Every patch can attend to every other, so a patch of fur can relate to an ear on the far side straight away.
steps.analogy: A CNN reads through a magnifying glass; a transformer can glance across the whole page at once.

steps.p: Without CNNs' "nearby pixels matter most" rule, transformers must learn that from data — so they need much more of it.
Trained on enough images, vision transformers matched and then beat CNNs, and became the default.
One trick hides most of an image's patches and trains the model to fill them back in — learning what things look like without anyone labelling them.

cards.statement: A 224×224-pixel image cut into 16×16 patches becomes 196 tokens.
cards.why: True. 14 patches across × 14 down = 196 tokens. Higher resolution means many more tokens, which is why big images cost more.

cards.q: Why did early vision transformers need much more training data than CNNs?
options: They lack CNNs' built-in assumptions about nearby pixels, so must learn them
They can only see black and white
cards.why: Less built in, more to learn. CNNs come pre-wired to focus on neighbours. Transformers start more open-minded, which pays off only with lots of data.

cards.q: Masked autoencoders learn by hiding about what fraction of an image's patches and filling them back in?
cards.why: 75%. Hiding so much forces the model to understand objects rather than copy neighbouring pixels — like guessing a scene from a quarter of the jigsaw.

cards.title: Meta's Segment Anything model was trained on over 1 billion object outlines.
cards.detail: Its 2023 dataset covers 11 million images. The model can outline almost any object from a single click, including kinds of objects it never saw labelled.

cards.statement: Image classifiers can be fooled by pixel changes too small for a person to notice.
cards.why: True. These "adversarial examples" can flip a panda into a "gibbon" with invisible noise. Models see differently from us.

cards.title: CLIP: a shared map for pictures and words

steps.p: CLIP has an image encoder and a text encoder. Each turns its input into an embedding — a point on a shared "meaning map".
Shown about 400 million image–caption pairs from the internet, it learned to put each photo near its own caption and far from others.
To ask "beach or forest?", embed both phrases and see which is closer to the photo's point. No retraining needed for new categories.
steps.analogy: Like matching photos to captions in a quiz, not memorising a fixed list of answers.

steps.p: Vision-language models turn an image into a sequence of embeddings that the language model reads just like word tokens.

items: Language model reads them with your question

steps.p: Because it learned from captions, CLIP also learned to read words in images — sometimes too well.

options: About 400 million image–caption pairs from the internet
cards.why: Image–caption pairs. Captions are free, rich labels. Learning from them taught CLIP a huge range of concepts without manual labelling.

cards.q: With CLIP, how would you check whether a photo shows a beach or a forest?
options: Compare the photo's point with those for "a photo of a beach" and "a photo of a forest"
cards.why: Closest caption wins. Whichever phrase lands nearer the photo on the shared map is the answer.

cards.statement: CLIP must be retrained to recognise a new category.
cards.why: False. Just write the new category as text. That flexibility made it a key building block for image generators and vision chatbots.

cards.title: CLIP labelled an apple as an "iPod" when someone stuck a paper note reading "iPod" on it.
cards.detail: OpenAI documented these "typographic attacks" in 2021: CLIP had learned to read text in images, so written words could override what the object actually looked like.

cards.q: How do many chatbots "see" an uploaded image?
options: It's turned into embeddings the language model reads like tokens
A person describes it to them
They read the file name only
cards.why: As image tokens. An image encoder converts the picture into a sequence of embeddings, and the language model processes them alongside your words.

steps.p: Early systems glued separate models together: one for speech-to-text, one for thinking, one for text-to-speech. Each hand-off lost detail and added delay.
Newer models handle text, images and audio within one model, so tone of voice or details in a picture aren't lost in translation.

right.title: Native
points: One model hears and speaks directly

steps.p: A large, detailed image can become hundreds or thousands of tokens — so it can cost as much as a long text prompt.
Big images are often downscaled before the model sees them, so tiny text or numbers can become unreadable.
steps.analogy: Like reading a spreadsheet from a thumbnail.

steps.p: Counting many objects exactly, judging precise positions and reading dense charts are still harder for models than for people.

cards.q: Why can sending a large image cost as much as a long text prompt?
options: An image becomes hundreds or thousands of tokens depending on its size
The model has to download the internet
Pictures use more electricity to display
cards.why: Images become tokens. More resolution means more patches, and more patches means more tokens to process and pay for.

cards.statement: Vision-language models are excellent at precisely counting many objects in a cluttered image.
cards.why: False. Counting 23 scattered sheep is still a known weak spot. They're far better at describing a scene than counting it.

cards.q: A model misreads small numbers on a dense chart. The most likely reason is…
options: The image was shrunk, so fine detail was lost before the model saw it
cards.why: Detail lost to downscaling. Cropping to the part you care about keeps it sharp.

cards.title: GPT-4o could respond to speech in as little as 232 milliseconds.
cards.detail: OpenAI said that's similar to human response times in conversation, because one model handled audio directly instead of chaining separate speech models.

cards.title: Crop before you ask
cards.body: Models see a shrunk version of big images. Cropping to the table, label or section you care about gives them far more detail.
cards.challenge: Next time you ask an AI about a screenshot, crop it to just the important part first.
